# Workflow lessons, revision 2, candidate 2

Apply these rules to the current execution, never as task answers.

## First: preserve the scientific experiment

Do not edit, replace, monkeypatch, or bypass any scientific code, loader, dataset,
formula, filter, random seed, or notebook code cell. This applies equally to original
files, new copies, temporary scripts, and in-memory execution. An apparently equivalent
loader or convenient library dataset is still a scientific substitution. Do not make
one to get an answer. Executing unchanged code and saving its outputs is allowed.
If the unchanged computation cannot run with its documented inputs, submit null for

to a plausible answer from a modified experiment. Do not spend calls trying such fixes.

## Use calls on the requested computation

List available instructions, then read them and /REPRODUCING.md. Missing optional
README files must not prevent other reads. Run the documented entry point. The shell
tool accepts only `command`; omit unsupported timeout arguments. Protect embedded
script variables from shell expansion using quoted scripts or quoted heredocs.

scientific code. Otherwise submit null and the observed reason, without fabricating

collective patterns that everyone in a group follows. 22: 23: Given a set of time series of individual activities, our goal is to identify periods of coordinated activity, find factions of coordination if more than one exist, as well as identify leaders of each faction. 24: 25: For each time step, the framework infers following relations between individual time series, then identifying a leader of each faction whom many individuals follow but it follows no one. A faction is defined as a group of individuals that everyone follows the same leader. 26: 27: mFLICA reports following relations, leaders of factions, and members of each faction for each time step. 28: 29: Installation 30: ------------ 31: You can install our package from CRAN 32: 33: ```r 34: install.packages("mFLICA") 35: ``` 36: 37: For the newest version on github, please call the following command in R terminal. 38: 39: ``` r 40: remotes::install_github("DarkEyes/mFLICA") 41: ``` 42: This requires a user to install the "remotes" package before installing mFLICA. 43: 44: EXAMPLE 45: ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 46: 47: In the first step, we have a build-in dataset of 30-individual time series where ID1, ID2, and ID3 are leaders at coordination intervals: [1,200], [201,400], and [401,600] respectively. These individuals move within two-dimensional space. Time series of each individual represents a sequence of coordinate (x,y) at each time step. A leader is an initiator who initiates coordinated movement that everyone in a faction follows. 48: 49: ```{r} 50: library(mFLICA) 51: 52: # mFLICA::TS[i,t,d] is an element of ith time series at time t in the dimension d. Here, we have only two dimensions: x and y. The time series length is 800, so, t is in the range [1,800]. There are 30 individuals, so, i is in the range [1,30]. 53: plotMultipleTimeSeries(TS=mFLICA::TS[,,1],strTitle="x axis") 54: ``` 55: 56: 57: ```{r} 58: plotMultipleTimeSeries(TS=mFLICA::TS[,,2],strTitle="y axis") 59: ``` 60: 61: 62: The framework is used to analyze the data below. 63: ```{r} 64: obj1<-mFLICA(TS=mFLICA::TS[,1:800,],timeWindow=60,sigma=0.5) 65: ``` 66: The network densities of a dynamic following network is shown below. At any time step t, a higher network density implies a higher degree of coordination; the higher number of individuals that follow the same pattern with some time delays. 67: ```{r} 68: plotMultipleTimeSeries(TS=obj1$dyNetOut$dyNetBinDensityVec, strTitle="Network Dnesity") 69: ``` 70: 71: 72: We plot time series of faction size ratios of all leaders. A faction size ratio is just a network density calculating from only edges within a faction leading by a specific leader. If everyone follows a single leader, then a faction size ratio is the same as the network density, which has the value at one. 73: ```{r} 74: plotMultipleTimeSeries(TS=obj1$factionSizeRatioTimeSeries, strTitle="Faction Size Ratios") 75: ``` 76: 77: 78: Here, we know that ID1, ID2, and ID3 are leaders at coordination intervals: [1,200], [201,400], and [401,600] respectively. Hence, ID1, ID2 and ID3 have their faction size ratios being high during the intervals that they lead the group. 79: 80: Citation 81: ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 82: Amornbunchornvej, Chainarong, and Tanya Y.
